title: Dalton Caldwell: Why low ambition kills venture-backed startups
summary: Dalton and Michael Seibel argue that aiming small is the hidden killer of venture-backed startups, because big missions attract customers, hires and investors who care. They stress that ambition must come with a simple, credible pitch rooted in real knowledge, and warn against funding-cycle noise and scenesters.

principles.text: Pair big ambition with a pitch built on intuitive, credible logical leaps.
principles.quote: a pitch where the logical leaps you are making are intuitive and that you are credible at making those logical leaps.

principles.text: Root ambition in things you actually know, and keep the leap of faith small.
principles.quote: you have to root it in things that you know about and make very simple low leap of faith arguments on how you'll be able to do it.

principles.text: Tell your ambitious story to everyone, constantly; it recruits team, money and believers.
principles.quote: And that simple story that is that ambitious and clearly he just told everyone that.

principles.text: Funding trends in the market can warp your sense of what a good idea is.
principles.quote: if you're keeping score on what's raising money, you can get really warped ideas about what good is.

principles.text: Pick ideas by their potential impact, not by whether they can raise a seed round.
principles.quote: Like whether it can raise a seed round is not the KPI.

principles.text: If you can't make your startup ambitious, work somewhere ambitious first; a low-ambition idea is a tarpit.
principles.quote: If you burn years of your life on something that you think is a waste of time in your heart of hearts that is a true tarpit.
